svg.text: A raw count tells you almost nothing until you know how many people it came from.

g.text: Hospital A reports 200 maternal deaths and Hospital B reports 20. Which is more dangerous?
You cannot say. Hospital A may deliver 40,000 women and Hospital B only 500. Per delivery, B is far worse.

svg.text: A big hospital always has bigger numbers. That is not the same as being less safe.

g.text: Incidence counts NEW cases in a period.
It measures the speed of a disease.
Prevalence counts ALL cases at a

svg.text: and tells you what services are needed.

g.text: People with HIV now live for decades,
so more of them are alive at any

svg.text: Rising prevalence is not always bad news.

g.text: If the risk fell from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in
1,000, that is one person in a thousand.

svg.text: WHO IS MISSING FROM THE DATA?

g.text: Facility records count only those who
reached the facility. The women who
died at home never appear in them

svg.text: Before believing any figure, ask three questions: out of how many, over what period, and who was left out.
Rates are written per 1,000 or per 100,000 so that places of different sizes can honestly be compared.
Good data collected badly is worse than no data, because it is believed.
